The Problem with Analysis Scripts
Code written during analysis tends to be:

One massive 500-line script with no structure
Variables named df2, df_final, df_final2, df_FINAL_USE_THIS
Hardcoded paths that only work on your laptop
No comments — you wrote it, you know what it does (for now)
Three months later: no idea what tmp3 is



For a capstone project that you might actually use in research:
write code as if a colleague needs to run it without you.

# ============================================================

library(phyloseq)
library(tidyverse)
library(here)

# 1. Load data -----------------------------------------------
ps <- readRDS(here("data", "raw", "hmp2_phyloseq.rds"))

# 2. QC & filtering ------------------------------------------
ps_clean <- prune_samples(sample_sums(ps) > 1000, ps)
ps_clean <- prune_taxa(taxa_sums(ps_clean) > 10, ps_clean)

# 3. Analysis ------------------------------------------------
ps_rare  <- rarefy_even_depth(ps_clean, rngseed = 42)
alpha    <- estimate_richness(ps_rare, measures = "Shannon")

# 4. Visualization -------------------------------------------
p <- ggplot(...) + ...

# 5. Save outputs --------------------------------------------
ggsave(here("results", "figures", "diversity_plot.pdf"), p,
       width = 7, height = 5)
write_tsv(da_taxa, here("results", "tables", "da_taxa.tsv"))

text:
Writing Functions — Don’t Repeat Yourself

# BAD — copy-pasted analysis per cell type
cd8_markers <- FindMarkers(seurat, ident.1 = "CD8 T", ...)
cd4_markers <- FindMarkers(seurat, ident.1 = "CD4 T", ...)
nk_markers  <- FindMarkers(seurat, ident.1 = "NK", ...)

# GOOD — write a function once
get_markers <- function(seurat_obj, cell_type,
                         min_pct = 0.25, logfc = 0.5) {
  FindMarkers(seurat_obj,
              ident.1         = cell_type,
              min.pct         = min_pct,
              logfc.threshold = logfc) |>
    as_tibble(rownames = "gene") |>
    mutate(cell_type = cell_type)
}

# Apply to all cell types
all_markers <- map_dfr(
  c("CD8 T", "CD4 T", "NK", "B cell", "Monocyte"),
  ~ get_markers(seurat, .x)
)

The AI Assistance Workflow
1. Describe your goal clearly (context + task + constraints)
         ↓
2. Get AI-generated code
         ↓
3. READ the code — understand every line
         ↓
4. Run it on a small subset first
         ↓
5. Check the output makes biological sense
         ↓
6. Ask AI to explain anything unclear
         ↓
7. Iterate






Non-negotiable


You are responsible for the code in your analysis.
AI can write it. You must understand it.
“The AI wrote it” is not an explanation in a methods section.

FindMarkers(seurat, ident.1 = levels(Idents(seurat))[1])

title: Network Analysis & Drug Repositioning
text:
The Limitation of Gene Lists
Every analysis we’ve done produces a gene list:

GWAS → prioritized genes
scRNA-seq → marker genes
Multi-omics → convergent genes


But genes don’t act alone.

A list of 200 DE genes tells you what is changing.
A network tells you how those genes are connected,
which ones are hubs, and what drugs might target the network.

title: Network Analysis & Drug Repositioning
text:
What Network Analysis Adds

Module detection — groups of co-expressed / co-regulated genes
Hub genes — highly connected nodes → often best drug targets
Shortest paths — how does signal propagate from receptor to effector?
Drug target mapping — which approved drugs hit nodes in this network?
Disease–drug similarity — repositioning based on network proximity

title: Network Analysis & Drug Repositioning
text:
STRINGdb — The Standard PPI Database

library(STRINGdb)
library(igraph)
library(tidyverse)
library(here)

# Initialize STRINGdb (human, high confidence)
string_db <- STRINGdb$new(
  version      = "11.5",
  species      = 9606,         # Homo sapiens
  score_threshold = 700,       # high confidence (0–1000)
  network_type = "full",
  input_directory = here("data", "raw", "string")
)

# Map your gene list to STRING IDs
candidate_genes <- read_tsv(here("results",
                                  "prioritized_genes.tsv"))

genes_mapped <- string_db$map(candidate_genes,
                               "gene",
                               removeUnmappedRows = TRUE)

# Get interaction network
ppi_network <- string_db$get_interactions(genes_mapped$STRING_id)
head(ppi_network)

title: Network Analysis & Drug Repositioning
text:
Build igraph Network

library(igraph)

# Create graph from PPI edges
g <- graph_from_data_frame(
  d        = ppi_network |>
    select(from = from, to = to, weight = combined_score),
  directed = FALSE,
  vertices = genes_mapped |>
    select(name = STRING_id, gene)
)

# Basic network statistics
cat("Nodes:", vcount(g), "\n")
cat("Edges:", ecount(g), "\n")
cat("Density:", round(edge_density(g), 4), "\n")

# Hub genes — highest degree
hub_genes <- sort(degree(g), decreasing = TRUE) |> head(20)
cat("Top hubs:\n")
print(hub_genes)

title: Network Analysis & Drug Repositioning
text:
Network Visualization

library(ggraph)
library(tidygraph)

# Convert to tidygraph
tg <- as_tbl_graph(g) |>
  mutate(
    degree      = centrality_degree(),
    betweenness = centrality_betweenness(),
    community   = as.factor(group_louvain())
  )

# Plot
ggraph(tg, layout = "fr") +
  geom_edge_link(aes(alpha = weight),
                 color    = "gray70",
                 show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_node_point(aes(size  = degree,
                      color = community)) +
  geom_node_text(aes(label = gene,
                     filter = degree > quantile(degree, 0.9)),
                 repel = TRUE, size = 3) +
  scale_size_continuous(range = c(2, 10)) +
  labs(title = "PPI network — prioritized GWAS genes",
       color = "Module") +
  theme_graph()

Druggability of Network Hubs

library(tidyverse)
library(here)

# Open Targets — drug-target associations database
# Download from https://platform.opentargets.org/downloads
ot_drugs <- read_parquet(
  here("data", "raw", "open_targets_drugs.parquet")
)

# Map network hubs to drug targets
hub_gene_names <- names(sort(degree(g), decreasing = TRUE))[1:50]

druggable_hubs <- ot_drugs |>
  filter(targetSymbol %in% hub_gene_names) |>
  select(gene       = targetSymbol,
         drug       = drugId,
         drug_name  = drugName,
         phase      = maximumClinicalTrialPhase,
         action     = actionType,
         indication = disease) |>
  arrange(desc(phase))

# Phase 3/4 drugs targeting our hub genes
druggable_hubs |>
  filter(phase >= 3) |>
  distinct(gene, drug_name, phase, action)

title: Network Analysis & Drug Repositioning
Network Analysis & Drug Repositioning
text:
The Connectivity Map Idea

Disease signature — genes UP in disease vs. control
Drug signature — genes UP/DOWN after drug treatment (L1000)
Key insight: if a drug’s signature is the reverse of the disease signature → the drug might reverse the disease transcriptome


First demonstrated: ibuprofen reverses aging gene expression signature.
Used to identify: thalidomide analogs for multiple myeloma, metformin for cancer.

title: Network Analysis & Drug Repositioning
text:
Running CMAP Query

library(cmapR)
library(here)

# Load L1000 GCTX file (CMap Phase II — 978 landmark genes)
ds <- parse_gctx(here("data", "raw",
                       "level5_beta_trt_cp_n720216x978.gctx"),
                 rid  = NULL,
                 cid  = NULL)

# Your disease signature
# Genes up in disease (from DESeq2 / scRNA-seq)
up_genes   <- c("IL6", "TNF", "CXCL8", "CCL2", "MMP9")
down_genes <- c("ADIPOQ", "PPARG", "IRS1", "GLUT4")

# Score each drug against your signature
# Kolmogorov-Smirnov enrichment test
ks_score <- function(drug_profile, up_set, down_set, n_total) {
  up_idx   <- which(names(drug_profile) %in% up_set)
  down_idx <- which(names(drug_profile) %in% down_set)

  ks_up   <- ks.test(up_idx,   1:n_total)$statistic
  ks_down <- ks.test(down_idx, 1:n_total)$statistic

  if (sign(ks_up) == sign(ks_down)) return(0)
  (ks_up - ks_down) / 2
}

title: Network Analysis & Drug Repositioning
text:
Visualizing CMAP Results

# Top repositioning candidates (negative score = disease reversal)
cmap_results |>
  arrange(connectivity_score) |>
  slice_head(n = 20) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = connectivity_score,
             y = reorder(drug_name, -connectivity_score),
             fill = connectivity_score < -0.5)) +
  geom_col() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("gray70", "#1D9E75"),
                    labels  = c("Weak", "Strong reversal")) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = -0.5, linetype = "dashed",
             color = "#D85A30") +
  labs(x     = "Connectivity score",
       y     = "Drug",
       fill  = "Reversal strength",
       title = "CMAP — top disease-reversing drugs") +
  theme_minimal()

MR as Causal Drug Target Validation

If the gene product is causally involved in disease (via MR),
modulating it pharmacologically should have a therapeutic effect.


library(TwoSampleMR)

# Example: Is PCSK9 causally linked to CAD?

# Instruments: GWAS SNPs for PCSK9 expression (cis-eQTL)

# Outcome: CAD GWAS
cad_outcome <- extract_outcome_data(
  snps     = pcsk9_instruments$SNP,
  outcomes = "ieu-a-7"
)

harmonised <- harmonise_data(pcsk9_instruments, cad_outcome)
mr_result  <- mr(harmonised)
mr_result

# If causal → PCSK9 inhibitors (evolocumab, alirocumab) should work

title: Advanced Single-cell Analysis: Trajectory & Cell–Cell Communication
text:
What Clustering Doesn’t Tell You
From last week — we can cluster cells and annotate them.
But biology is dynamic, not static:

Stem cells → progenitors → differentiated cells
Naive T cells → activated → effector → exhausted
Fibroblasts → myofibroblasts → senescent cells



Pseudotime trajectory analysis asks:
Given a snapshot of cells, can we infer the order and direction of differentiation?

text:
The Core Idea
scRNA-seq is a snapshot:
All cells captured at the same moment

But cells are at different stages of a process:
Cell A: early progenitor
Cell B: mid-differentiation
Cell C: terminal state

Pseudotime: order cells along a trajectory
             based on transcriptional similarity

library(monocle3)

library(tidyverse)

# Convert to CellDataSet (Monocle3 format)

# Preprocessing

                    verbose = FALSE)

# Learn trajectory graph

text:
The Idea Behind RNA Velocity
For any gene in a cell:

Unspliced pre-mRNA (u):  newly transcribed → proxy for FUTURE state
Spliced mRNA (s):         mature message   → CURRENT state

If u > expected given s:  gene is being upregulated → cell moving in that direction
If u < expected given s:  gene is being downregulated → cell moving away

RNA velocity predicts the direction and speed of cell state transitions —
like an arrow on the UMAP showing where each cell is heading.

Interpreting Velocity Plots
What to look for:

Arrows pointing toward a cluster → that cluster is a terminal state (attractor)
Arrows pointing away from a cluster → that cluster is a progenitor
Circular arrows → cycling cells (proliferating)
Scattered / no arrows → cells in a stable state or not enough signal








Caveat


RNA velocity requires unspliced count information (velocyto loom files).
Not all public datasets provide this.
When not available: use Monocle3 pseudotime as the alternative.

Cells Don’t Work Alone

Cytokines — IL-6, TNF-α, IFN-γ → paracrine signaling
Growth factors — EGF, VEGF, FGF → receptor–ligand pairs
Extracellular matrix — integrins, collagen → structural signals
Direct contact — Notch–Jagged, E-cadherin


scRNA-seq lets us infer these interactions from expression data:

If cell type A expresses ligand X and cell type B expresses receptor Y,
and X–Y is a known signaling pair,
→ infer that A is signaling to B via X–Y.

What WMS Gives You

Functional profiling — which metabolic pathways are active (HUMAnN3)

title: Metagenomics II: Whole Metagenome Shotgun (WMS)
text:
How MetaPhlAn4 Works
WMS reads
    ↓
Map against clade-specific marker genes
(~5.1 million markers from ~99,000 genomes)
    ↓
Estimate relative abundance at each taxonomic level:
Kingdom → Phylum → Class → Order → Family → Genus → Species → Strain

Advantages over 16S: - No PCR amplification bias - Species and strain level resolution - Includes viruses, fungi, archaea

library(tidyverse)

                       skip = 1)

  filter(str_detect(`#clade_name`, "s__"),
         !str_detect(`#clade_name`, "t__")) |>
  mutate(species = str_extract(`#clade_name`,
                                "s__[^|]+$") |>
           str_remove("s__") |>
           str_replace("_", " "))

# Wide to long
species_long <- species |>
  pivot_longer(-c(`#clade_name`, NCBI_tax_id, species),
               names_to  = "sample",
               values_to = "relative_abundance")

Antimicrobial Resistance Genes in the Gut

The gut microbiome is a reservoir of AMR genes (the resistome)
Antibiotic exposure → selection → enrichment of resistant strains
Horizontal gene transfer → spread between commensal and pathogenic bacteria
Clinical relevance: pre-treatment resistome may predict ICU infection outcomes, C. diff. colonization risk, and post-transplant infection

  group_by(sample, drug_class) |>
  summarise(total_rpk = sum(reads_per_kbp), .groups = "drop")

  group_by(sample) |>
  summarise(
    n_genes  = n_distinct(gene_family),
    total    = sum(reads_per_kbp)

text:
The Regulatory Genome
Only ~2% of the genome codes for proteins.
The other 98%? Largely regulatory.

Promoters — near TSS, where transcription initiates
Enhancers — distal elements, can be megabases away
Insulators — block enhancer–promoter interactions
Silencers — repress transcription



~90% of GWAS hits are non-coding.
To understand what they do, we need to know which regulatory elements are active
in which cell types — and how they contact their target genes.

title: Epigenomics II: Chromatin Accessibility & 3D Genome
text:
Chromatin Accessibility — The Key Readout
Closed chromatin:  DNA wrapped tightly around histones → inaccessible
                   [H][H][H][DNA][H][H][H]
                   Transcription factors cannot bind
                   Gene is OFF

Open chromatin:    nucleosome-depleted region → accessible
                   [H]         [H]
                   Transcription factors can bind
                   Gene is (potentially) ON

Open chromatin = active regulatory elements
→ cell-type-specific gene regulation

title: Epigenomics II: Chromatin Accessibility & 3D Genome
text:
How ATAC-seq Works
Nuclei isolation
    ↓
Tn5 transposase treatment
(cuts & inserts sequencing adapters ONLY in open chromatin)
    ↓
PCR amplification
    ↓
Short-read sequencing
    ↓
Reads pile up at open chromatin → "peaks"

Advantages: - Works on 500–50,000 cells (vs. DNase-seq needing millions) - Single-cell compatible (scATAC-seq) - Fast, cheap, highly reproducible

ATAC-seq Analysis Workflow
Raw FASTQ
    │
    ├── 1. QC & trimming         → FastQC, Trimmomatic
    ├── 2. Alignment             → Bowtie2 → hg38
    ├── 3. Post-alignment QC     → TSS enrichment, fragment size
    ├── 4. Peak calling          → MACS2
    ├── 5. Differential peaks    → DESeq2 on peak counts
    ├── 6. TF motif analysis     → chromVAR, HOMER
    └── 7. GWAS integration      → overlap GWAS hits with peaks






Note


Steps 1–4 require a Linux server (pre-computed for this class).
We start from peak files in R.

title: Epigenomics II: Chromatin Accessibility & 3D Genome
text:
Why 3D Structure Matters
DNA in the nucleus is not linear — it folds into a hierarchy:
Chromosome territory
    └── Compartment A/B (active/inactive, ~Mb scale)
            └── TAD (Topologically Associating Domain, ~100 kb–1 Mb)
                    └── Loop (enhancer–promoter contact, ~10–100 kb)

Clinical relevance:

TAD boundary disruption → new enhancer–gene contacts → oncogene activation
(e.g., PDGFRA activation in glioma by TAD reorganization)
Loop formation = enhancer–promoter contact = gene activation
GWAS hit in an enhancer → which gene’s promoter does it contact?

title: Epigenomics II: Chromatin Accessibility & 3D Genome
text:
Hi-C — Measuring 3D Contacts
Crosslink cells (formaldehyde)
    ↓
Restriction enzyme digestion
    ↓
Proximity ligation (nearby DNA ligated)
    ↓
Sequencing → pairs of genomic loci that were in contact
    ↓
Contact matrix: genomic bins × bins → interaction frequency

title: Epigenomics II: Chromatin Accessibility & 3D Genome
text:
TAD Calling

library(HiCcompare)

# TAD boundaries — insulation score method
# Dips in insulation score = TAD boundaries

insulation_score <- function(mat, window = 10) {
  n <- nrow(mat)
  scores <- numeric(n)
  for (i in (window+1):(n-window)) {
    upstream   <- mat[max(1, i-window):(i-1),
                     max(1, i-window):(i-1)]
    downstream <- mat[i:min(n, i+window),
                     i:min(n, i+window)]
    cross      <- mat[max(1, i-window):(i-1),
                     i:min(n, i+window)]
    scores[i]  <- mean(cross) / sqrt(mean(upstream) * mean(downstream))
  }
  scores
}

ins <- insulation_score(as.matrix(mat))

# TAD boundaries = local minima in insulation score

title: Spatial Transcriptomics
section: The Problem with Everything We’ve Done So Far
text:
The Problem with Everything We’ve Done So Far



Method
What we lose




Bulk RNA-seq
Cell type identity, spatial context


scRNA-seq (W8–W9)
Where in the tissue?


GWAS (W2–W3)
Cell type, tissue architecture




The fundamental problem:
Dissociating tissue into single cells destroys the spatial information.
You know what cells are doing — but not where, next to what, and in which microenvironment.

title: Spatial Transcriptomics
text:
What Spatial Transcriptomics Adds


scRNA-seq tells you:

This is a macrophage
It’s in an inflammatory state
It’s talking to a T cell


Spatial adds:

This macrophage is at the tumor invasion front
It’s 5 cell-widths from a blood vessel
The neighboring tumor cells are hypoxic




For a pathologist or oncologist, this is exactly how you think about tissue.
Spatial transcriptomics is digital pathology with transcriptomics layered on top.

title: Spatial Transcriptomics
text:
Clinical Scenarios Where This Matters

Tumor microenvironment — immune exclusion zone vs. inflamed phenotype → immunotherapy response
Tissue borders — where does normal end and dysplasia begin? Molecularly.
Fibrosis — which cells drive progression at the fibrotic front?
Brain — layer-specific gene expression in neurodegeneration
Gut — crypt-villus axis disruption in IBD
Cardiac — spatial heterogeneity in ischemic zones

title: Spatial Transcriptomics
text:
How Visium Works
Fresh-frozen tissue section (10 µm)
         ↓
Placed on capture array
(6,500 spots, each 55 µm, containing barcoded oligos)
         ↓
Permeabilization → mRNA released → captured by oligos
         ↓
cDNA synthesis + sequencing
         ↓
Each spot: ~10–20 cells + (x, y) coordinates + expression profile
         ↓
H&E image aligned to array

The result: a gene expression matrix where every row has a tissue coordinate.

text:
The Data Structure
Seurat object with spatial data:
├── counts matrix   (spots × genes)  e.g., 3,000 spots × 30,000 genes
├── spot coordinates (x, y) on tissue
├── H&E image
└── scalefactors    (pixel → µm conversion)

library(Seurat)
library(here)

# Load 10x Visium output
visium <- Load10X_Spatial(
  data.dir   = here("data", "raw", "visium_output"),
  filename   = "filtered_feature_bc_matrix.h5",
  assay      = "Spatial",
  slice      = "slice1",
  filter.matrix = TRUE
)

visium

text:
Overview
Raw Visium data
    │
    ├── 1. QC           → filter low-quality spots
    ├── 2. Normalization → SCTransform
    ├── 3. Dim reduction → PCA → UMAP
    ├── 4. Clustering   → spatial domains
    ├── 5. SVGs         → spatially variable genes
    ├── 6. Deconvolution → cell type per spot
    └── 7. Integration  → scRNA-seq reference

title: Spatial Transcriptomics
text:
Step 1: QC

# Mitochondrial gene percentage
visium[["percent.mt"]] <- PercentageFeatureSet(visium,
                                               pattern = "^MT-")

# Visualize QC metrics on tissue
SpatialFeaturePlot(visium,
                   features = c("nCount_Spatial",
                                "nFeature_Spatial",
                                "percent.mt"))


# Filter spots
visium <- subset(visium,
                 nCount_Spatial   > 500    &
                 nFeature_Spatial > 200    &
                 percent.mt       < 25)

cat("Spots remaining:", ncol(visium), "\n")

title: Spatial Transcriptomics
text:
Step 2: Normalization — SCTransform

# SCTransform — accounts for technical variation
# (sequencing depth varies across spots)
visium <- SCTransform(visium,
                      assay      = "Spatial",
                      verbose    = FALSE,
                      vars.to.regress = "percent.mt")







Why not standard normalization?


Spatial data has strong sequencing depth variation across the tissue section
(edge spots often have fewer counts).
SCTransform handles this better than simple log-normalization.

title: Spatial Transcriptomics
text:
Step 3: Dimensionality Reduction & Clustering

visium <- RunPCA(visium, assay = "SCT", verbose = FALSE)
visium <- FindNeighbors(visium, reduction = "pca", dims = 1:30)
visium <- FindClusters(visium, verbose = FALSE, resolution = 0.5)
visium <- RunUMAP(visium, reduction = "pca", dims = 1:30)

# Plot clusters in UMAP space AND on tissue
p1 <- DimPlot(visium, reduction = "umap", label = TRUE)
p2 <- SpatialDimPlot(visium, label = TRUE, label.size = 3)

p1 + p2


Key question: do the UMAP clusters correspond to anatomical regions?
If yes → the spatial domains are transcriptionally distinct.

Step 4: Spatially Variable Genes (SVGs)
Which genes vary across tissue space — not just between clusters, but continuously?

library(NNSVG)

# NNSVG: fast, scalable SVG detection
# Fits a spatial model per gene
nnsvg_results <- nnsvg(
  x        = counts(visium),
  coords   = spatialCoords(visium),
  n_threads = 4
)

# Top SVGs
top_svgs <- nnsvg_results |>
  arrange(desc(LR_stat)) |>
  slice_head(n = 20)

SpatialFeaturePlot(visium,
                   features = top_svgs$gene_name[1:6],
                   ncol = 3)

title: Spatial Transcriptomics
section: Step 5: Deconvolution — Cell Types per Spot
text:
Step 5: Deconvolution — Cell Types per Spot
Each Visium spot contains 10–20 cells → what mix of cell types?

library(STdeconvolve)

# Reference: single-cell RNA-seq from same tissue type
# (from W8–W9 analysis — this is why sc comes first!)
counts_spatial <- GetAssayData(visium, slot = "counts",
                               assay = "Spatial")

# Run deconvolution
ldaOut <- fitLDA(t(as.matrix(counts_spatial)),
                 Ks = seq(4, 9, by = 1))

# Optimal K
optLDA <- optimalModel(models = ldaOut, opt = "min")
results <- getBetaTheta(optLDA,
                        perc.filt = 0.05,
                        betaScale = 1000)

# Map cell type proportions back to tissue
vizAllTopics(theta        = results$theta,
             pos          = spatialCoords(visium),
             topicOrder   = seq(ncol(results$theta)),
             topicCols    = rainbow(ncol(results$theta)))

# Transfer cell type labels from scRNA-seq reference

# Load your W8-W9 scRNA-seq reference

# Find anchors between spatial and single-cell data

  reference      = sc_ref,

# Transfer labels

  anchorset    = anchors,
  refdata      = sc_ref$celltype,
  prediction.assay = TRUE,
  weight.reduction = visium[["pca"]],
  dims         = 1:30

visium[["predictions"]] <- predictions

text:
Cell–Cell Communication in Spatial Context

library(CellChat)

# Unlike standard CellChat (W9), spatial CellChat
# only considers cells within a defined distance

cellchat <- createCellChat(
  object   = visium,
  meta     = visium@meta.data,
  group.by = "predicted.celltype",
  datatype = "spatial",
  coordinates = GetTissueCoordinates(visium),
  spatial.factors = list(ratio = 0.1, tol = 0.08)
)

cellchat <- setIdent(cellchat, ident.use = "predicted.celltype")







Spatial constraint


Standard cell–cell communication assumes all cells can talk to all cells.
Spatial CellChat only allows interactions between physically neighboring spots — far more biologically realistic.

title: Genome-wide Association Studies (GWAS) & Post-GWAS
text:
GWAS Is Directly Clinical

Drug target validation — GWAS hits are 2× more likely to succeed in clinical trials
Disease subtyping — same phenotype, different genetic architecture → different treatment
Risk stratification — polygenic risk scores in preventive medicine (W3)
Comorbidity understanding — shared genetic architecture between diseases
Mendelian randomization — causal inference without RCT



If you read a Nature Medicine paper in 2024, there’s a good chance GWAS data is somewhere in it.

title: Genome-wide Association Studies (GWAS) & Post-GWAS
text:
What GWAS Actually Asks

“Which genetic variants are more common in people with disease X than in healthy controls?”


Compare allele frequencies at millions of SNPs simultaneously
No prior hypothesis about which gene — agnostic, genome-wide
Result: list of associated loci, not causal genes (yet)







SNP


Single Nucleotide Polymorphism — a single base difference at a given position in the genome.
~10 million common SNPs exist in humans; GWAS arrays typically genotype 500K–5M.

title: Genome-wide Association Studies (GWAS) & Post-GWAS
text:
GWAS Study Design
Participants
├── Cases   (n = 5,000+)   patients with disease
└── Controls (n = 10,000+) matched healthy individuals
         ↓
Genotyping array (SNP chip)
         ↓
Quality Control
         ↓
Statistical testing (per-SNP logistic regression)
         ↓
Results → Manhattan plot

Sample size matters enormously.
Early GWAS (n ~2,000) found almost nothing.
Modern biobank GWAS (n ~500,000) finds hundreds of loci.

title: Genome-wide Association Studies (GWAS) & Post-GWAS
text:
Population Stratification — The Key Confounder


If cases and controls differ in ancestry, any ancestry-associated variant looks like a disease hit.
Solution: Principal Component Analysis (PCA) on genotype data → include top PCs as covariates in the model.

# Model with PC adjustment
glm(disease ~ SNP + PC1 + PC2 + 
    PC3 + PC4 + PC5 + age + sex,
    family = binomial)







Always report your ancestry


Mixing populations without correction = false positives.
Restricting to one ancestry = limits generalizability (a real ongoing problem in the field).

title: Genome-wide Association Studies (GWAS) & Post-GWAS
text:
The Significance Threshold — Why 5×10⁻⁸?
Not arbitrary:

~1 million independent tests in the genome (after LD pruning)
Bonferroni: 0.05 / 1,000,000 = 5×10⁻⁸
Genome-wide significance: p < 5×10⁻⁸
Suggestive: p < 1×10⁻⁵







For reviewers


A “nearly significant” GWAS hit at p = 10⁻⁶ is not significant.
Replication in an independent cohort is the gold standard.

title: Genome-wide Association Studies (GWAS) & Post-GWAS
text:
The QQ Plot — Diagnosing Inflation

# QQ plot
qq(gwas_results$P,
   main = "QQ Plot — observed vs expected -log10(p)")


Perfect: points follow the diagonal, then deviate at the tail
Inflated (λ > 1.05): all points above diagonal → stratification not corrected
Deflated (λ < 0.95): overly conservative QC → lost power


# Calculate genomic inflation factor (lambda)
chisq <- qchisq(gwas_results$P, df = 1, lower.tail = FALSE)
lambda <- median(chisq) / qchisq(0.5, df = 1)
cat("Genomic inflation factor λ =", round(lambda, 3))

title: Genome-wide Association Studies (GWAS) & Post-GWAS
text:
The Problem with GWAS Hits
A GWAS hit is rarely the causal variant.
rs1234567  p = 3×10⁻²⁴   ← lead SNP (what GWAS finds)
    │
    ├── rs1234568  r² = 0.98   
    ├── rs1234591  r² = 0.95   ← one of these is actually causal
    └── rs1234612  r² = 0.91   
    
(all in high linkage disequilibrium — inherited together)
Post-GWAS workflow: 1. Fine-mapping — narrow down the credible set 2. Functional annotation — is it in a regulatory element? 3. Gene prioritization — which gene does it affect? 4. eQTL colocalization — does it regulate gene expression?

library(LDlinkR)

# Get LD between variants in a region
ld_matrix <- LDmatrix(
  snps  = c("rs1234567", "rs1234568", "rs1234591"),
  pop   = "CEU",           # 1000 Genomes population
  r2d   = "r2",
  token = "your_token"     # free at ldlink.nci.nih.gov
)

# LD proxy search

  snp   = "rs1234567",
  pop   = "CEU",
  r2d   = "r2",
  token = "your_token"
)

title: Genome-wide Association Studies (GWAS) & Post-GWAS
text:
Fine-Mapping — Credible Sets

library(susieR)

# SuSiE: Sum of Single Effects model
# Produces a credible set of variants likely containing the causal SNP
susie_fit <- susie(
  X = genotype_matrix,    # n_samples × n_snps
  y = phenotype_vector,
  L = 10                  # max number of causal signals
)

# 95% credible set
credible_set <- susie_get_cs(susie_fit, coverage = 0.95)


Fine-mapping shrinks from 200 correlated SNPs to a credible set of 5–20 most likely causal.

eQTL Colocalization — Connecting SNP to Gene
eQTL: expression QTL — a variant that affects gene expression level

library(coloc)

# Test whether GWAS signal and eQTL signal share the same causal variant
coloc_result <- coloc.abf(
  dataset1 = list(pvalues = gwas_pvals,
                  N       = 150000,
                  type    = "cc",     # case-control
                  s       = 0.3),     # proportion cases
  dataset2 = list(pvalues = eqtl_pvals,
                  N       = 500,
                  type    = "quant")  # quantitative (expression)
)

coloc_result$summary
# PP.H4: probability that GWAS and eQTL share the same causal variant

PP.H4 > 0.8 → strong evidence for colocalization → that gene is likely the target.

title: Genome-wide Association Studies (GWAS) & Post-GWAS
text:
Mendelian Randomization — Causal Inference

“Does elevated LDL cause coronary artery disease, or are they just correlated?”

Genetic variants → LDL levels → CAD
(instrument)       (exposure)    (outcome)

library(TwoSampleMR)

# Instrument: GWAS SNPs for LDL
exposure_dat <- extract_instruments("ieu-a-300")  # LDL GWAS

# Outcome: CAD GWAS
outcome_dat  <- extract_outcome_data(
  snps       = exposure_dat$SNP,
  outcomes   = "ieu-a-7"       # CAD GWAS
)

# Harmonize and run MR
dat    <- harmonise_data(exposure_dat, outcome_dat)
result <- mr(dat)


MR uses genetic variants as “natural randomization” — immune to confounding by lifestyle, SES, etc.

title: Genome-wide Association Studies (GWAS) & Post-GWAS
section: What to Interpret from a Locus
text:
What to Interpret from a Locus
For any GWAS hit, ask:

Is it replicated? — in an independent cohort?
What’s the LD structure? — how many SNPs in the credible set?
What’s the functional context? — coding, regulatory, eQTL?
Which gene? — nearest gene ≠ causal gene
What’s the effect size? — OR / beta; GWAS hits are usually small
Any drug target? — is the gene druggable?

title: Genome-wide Association Studies (GWAS) & Post-GWAS
text:
What GWAS Cannot Tell You

Causality — association ≠ causation (MR helps, but has assumptions)
Rare variants — standard GWAS misses MAF < 1% (need WES/WGS)
Mechanism — a hit at an enhancer tells you something regulates something
Diverse populations — most GWAS are European-ancestry; results may not transfer
Gene-environment interaction — static genetic associations miss dynamic biology



GWAS is the beginning of the story, not the end.
This is exactly why the rest of the semester exists.

title: Genome-wide Association Studies (GWAS) & Post-GWAS

text:
GWAS + The Rest of the Curriculum
GWAS hit identified
    │
    ├─ W4–W5  Epigenomics    → Is the hit in an active enhancer?
    ├─ W6–W7  Metagenomics   → Does the microbiome mediate the effect?
    ├─ W8–W9  scRNA-seq      → Which cell type expresses the gene?
    ├─ W10    Spatial        → Where in the tissue?
    ├─ W11    Multi-omics    → Convergent evidence across layers
    └─ W12    Drug target    → Is there a druggable molecule?
GWAS is the entry point — everything else gives it biological meaning.

title: Polygenic Risk Scores (PRS)
section: The Limitation of Single GWAS Hits
text:
The Limitation of Single GWAS Hits
From last week:

GWAS finds variants with p < 5×10⁻⁸
But most complex diseases are influenced by thousands of variants
Each with a tiny effect size (OR 1.02–1.15)
No single variant is clinically useful alone



PRS aggregates the effects of thousands of SNPs into a single score per individual.

title: Polygenic Risk Scores (PRS)
text:
What a PRS Looks Like
Individual A:
  rs1001  risk allele × 0.03
+ rs2045  risk allele × 0.02
+ rs8821  non-risk    × 0.00
+ ... (thousands more)
─────────────────────────────
= PRS: 1.42  (top 20% of population → 3× increased risk)

Clinically:
One number, derived from a saliva sample at birth,
that captures lifetime genetic predisposition to a disease.

title: Polygenic Risk Scores (PRS)
section: Clinical Utility — Where PRS Is Already Used
text:
Clinical Utility — Where PRS Is Already Used

Coronary artery disease — PRS identifies high-risk individuals who benefit from early statin therapy
Breast cancer — PRS improves risk stratification beyond BRCA1/2
Type 2 diabetes — PRS + lifestyle factors → personalized prevention
Atrial fibrillation — PRS predicts incident AF beyond clinical risk scores
Prostate cancer — PRS guides screening intensity








The key point for clinicians


PRS adds information on top of traditional risk factors — age, BMI, family history, biomarkers.
The question is always: does it change clinical management?

title: Polygenic Risk Scores (PRS)
text:
Method 1: C+T (Clumping and Thresholding)
The simplest approach:
1. Clumping: keep only one SNP per LD block
   (remove correlated SNPs → independent signals only)

2. Thresholding: keep SNPs below a p-value cutoff
   (e.g., p < 0.05, p < 0.01, p < 5×10⁻⁸)

3. PRS = Σ (effect size × allele count)

library(bigsnpr)

# C+T with PRSice2 (via system call) or bigsnpr
obj.bigsnp <- snp_attach(here("data", "raw", "target.rds"))
G <- obj.bigsnp$genotypes

# Clumping
ind.keep <- snp_clumping(
  G,
  infos.chr = obj.bigsnp$map$chromosome,
  infos.pos = obj.bigsnp$map$physical.pos,
  S         = abs(sumstats$Z),     # use Z-score for clumping
  thr.r2    = 0.1,
  size      = 500
)

title: Polygenic Risk Scores (PRS)
text:
Method 2: LDpred2 — The Current Standard
Accounts for LD structure more accurately using a Bayesian framework:

library(bigsnpr)

# Step 1: Match summary stats to target genotypes
sumstats <- snp_match(sumstats, obj.bigsnp$map)

# Step 2: Compute LD reference matrix
POS2 <- snp_asGeneticPos(
  infos.chr = obj.bigsnp$map$chromosome,
  infos.pos = obj.bigsnp$map$physical.pos,
  dir       = here("data", "raw", "genetic_maps")
)

corr <- snp_cor(G, ind.col = sumstats$`_NUM_ID_`,
                infos.pos = POS2, size = 3 / 1000)

# Step 3: LDpred2-auto (no tuning needed)
ldsc <- with(sumstats,
             snp_ldsc(ld_score, ld_size = nrow(G),
                      chi2  = (beta / beta_se)^2,
                      sample_size = n_eff))

h2_est <- ldsc[["h2"]]

multi_auto <- snp_ldpred2_auto(
  corr, sumstats, h2_init = h2_est,
  vec_p_init = seq_log(1e-4, 0.2, length.out = 30),
  burn_in = 500, num_iter = 500, report_step = 20
)

title: Polygenic Risk Scores (PRS)
text:
Method 3: PRSice2 — Practical Workhorse

# PRSice2 is a command-line tool
# Call from R via system()
system(paste(
  "PRSice",
  "--base",    here("data", "raw", "sumstats.txt"),
  "--target",  here("data", "raw", "target_plink"),
  "--binary-target", "T",
  "--pheno",   here("data", "raw", "phenotype.txt"),
  "--cov",     here("data", "raw", "covariates.txt"),
  "--out",     here("results", "prsice_output"),
  "--thread",  4
))







Note


PRSice2 automatically optimizes the p-value threshold and produces
a bar chart, high-resolution plot, and quantile plot.

title: Polygenic Risk Scores (PRS)
text:
Comparing Methods








Method
Pros
Cons




C+T
Fast, interpretable
Loses information, arbitrary threshold


LDpred2
Best predictive accuracy, principled
Slower, needs LD reference


PRSice2
Easy to use, good visualization
Threshold-based


PRS-CS
Handles diverse ancestries better
Needs Python




For clinical research: LDpred2 or PRSice2.
For multi-ancestry: PRS-CS or PRS-CSx.

title: Polygenic Risk Scores (PRS)
text:
Key Performance Metrics

library(tidyverse)

# Load PRS scores + phenotype
prs_data <- read_tsv(here("results", "prsice_output.best")) |>
  left_join(phenotype, by = "IID")

# Nagelkerke R² — variance explained by PRS
library(DescTools)

# Null model (covariates only)
null_model <- glm(disease ~ age + sex + PC1 + PC2 + PC3 + PC4 + PC5,
                  data   = prs_data,
                  family = binomial)

# Full model (covariates + PRS)
full_model <- glm(disease ~ PRS + age + sex + PC1 + PC2 + PC3 + PC4 + PC5,
                  data   = prs_data,
                  family = binomial)

r2_prs <- PseudoR2(full_model, "Nagelkerke") -
          PseudoR2(null_model, "Nagelkerke")
cat("R² explained by PRS:", round(r2_prs, 4), "\n")

title: Polygenic Risk Scores (PRS)
text:
AUC and Discrimination

library(pROC)

# ROC curve — does PRS improve discrimination?
roc_null <- roc(prs_data$disease,
                predict(null_model, type = "response"))

roc_full <- roc(prs_data$disease,
                predict(full_model, type = "response"))

# Compare AUCs
roc.test(roc_null, roc_full)

# Plot
ggroc(list(Clinical = roc_null,
           `Clinical + PRS` = roc_full)) +
  labs(title = "ROC: Does PRS improve prediction?",
       color  = "Model") +
  theme_minimal()

title: Polygenic Risk Scores (PRS)
text:
Quantile Plot — Clinical Interpretation

# Divide PRS into deciles
prs_data <- prs_data |>
  mutate(prs_decile = ntile(PRS, 10))

# Odds ratio per decile vs. middle decile (reference)
or_by_decile <- prs_data |>
  group_by(prs_decile) |>
  summarise(
    n_cases    = sum(disease == 1),
    n_controls = sum(disease == 0)
  ) |>
  mutate(
    OR = (n_cases / n_controls) /
         (n_cases[prs_decile == 5] / n_controls[prs_decile == 5])
  )

ggplot(or_by_decile, aes(prs_decile, OR)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#185FA5") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "PRS decile",
       y = "Odds Ratio vs. middle decile",
       title = "Disease risk by PRS decile") +
  theme_minimal()

title: Polygenic Risk Scores (PRS)
section: PRS in Diverse Populations — A Real Problem
text:
PRS in Diverse Populations — A Real Problem

Most GWAS (and therefore PRS) are trained on European-ancestry individuals
PRS built on European GWAS performs 4–5× worse in African-ancestry populations
Applying biased PRS clinically could widen health disparities
Active research: PRS-CSx, multi-ancestry GWAS meta-analysis








For Korean patients


Korean-specific GWAS (KoGES, KCHIP, TOPMed Korean) exist for major diseases.
Always check whether the base GWAS matches your target population’s ancestry.

title: Polygenic Risk Scores (PRS)
text:
What PRS Cannot Do

Causality — high PRS ≠ will develop disease
Rare variants — PRS misses high-penetrance rare variants (BRCA1/2, Lynch syndrome)
Gene–environment interaction — genetic risk can be modified by lifestyle
Replace clinical judgment — PRS is one input, not a diagnosis

title: Polygenic Risk Scores (PRS)
text:
PRS + Clinical Risk Scores

# Example: CAD risk — PRS vs. traditional risk factors
library(tidyverse)

# Framingham Risk Score + PRS
combined_model <- glm(
  cad ~ PRS + age + sex + total_chol + hdl_chol +
        systolic_bp + smoking + diabetes,
  data   = prs_data,
  family = binomial
)

# Net reclassification index
library(PredictABEL)
reclassification(
  data         = prs_data,
  cOutcome     = "cad",
  predrisk1    = predict(null_model, type = "response"),
  predrisk2    = predict(combined_model, type = "response"),
  cutoff       = c(0, 0.1, 0.2, 1)
)

# Match summary stats to target SNPs

                           ind.col = ind[!is.na(ind)])

title: Epigenomics I: DNA Methylation
text:
Beyond the DNA Sequence
Same genome. Different cell types. Different functions.
Neuron  ─── DNA ──→  expresses NEFL, SNAP25, SYP
Hepatocyte ─ DNA ──→  expresses ALB, CYP3A4, F2
T cell  ─── DNA ──→  expresses CD3E, CD8A, GZMB

The genome is the same. The epigenome is different.
Epigenomics studies the regulatory layer on top of the DNA sequence: - DNA methylation - Histone modifications - Chromatin accessibility (W5) - 3D genome organization (W5)

title: Epigenomics I: DNA Methylation
text:
Why Epigenomics for Clinicians?

Cancer — global hypomethylation + gene-specific hypermethylation → tumor suppressor silencing
Aging — epigenetic clocks predict biological age, mortality, disease risk
Drug response — methylation status of promoters predicts chemotherapy sensitivity
Developmental disorders — imprinting diseases (Prader-Willi, Angelman)
Liquid biopsy — cell-free DNA methylation → tissue of origin for cancer detection

title: Epigenomics I: DNA Methylation
text:
The Biology
CpG dinucleotide:  5'─C─G─3'
                   3'─G─C─5'

Methylation:   5'─[m]C─G─3'   (5-methylcytosine)

Maintained by: DNMT1 (maintenance methyltransferase)
Written by:    DNMT3A / DNMT3B (de novo)
Erased by:     TET enzymes (oxidation → demethylation)

Effect on gene expression: - Promoter methylation → gene silencing - Gene body methylation → associated with active transcription (context-dependent) - Enhancer methylation → reduced enhancer activity

title: Epigenomics I: DNA Methylation
text:
CpG Islands, Shores, and Shelves
                shore    CGI      shore
──────────────[====][===========][====]──────────────
              shelf                     shelf

CpG Island (CGI): high CpG density, usually unmethylated in normal tissue
Shore (0–2 kb):   variable methylation, most disease-relevant
Shelf (2–4 kb):   lower CpG density
Open sea:         remaining genome






Clinically important


Most cancer-associated methylation changes happen at CGI shores, not the islands themselves.

rgSet

# Check: should see ~935,000 probes (EPIC) or ~485,000 (450K)

title: Epigenomics I: DNA Methylation
text:
Step 2: QC

# QC report
qcReport(rgSet,
         sampNames = targets$Sample_Name,
         sampGroups = targets$Sample_Group,
         pdf       = here("results", "qc_report.pdf"))

# Detection p-values — probes with p > 0.01 are unreliable
detP <- detectionP(rgSet)
failed <- detP > 0.01
cat("Failed probes per sample:\n")
colSums(failed)

# Remove samples with > 1% failed probes
keep <- colMeans(failed) < 0.01
rgSet <- rgSet[, keep]
cat("Samples remaining:", ncol(rgSet), "\n")

title: Epigenomics I: DNA Methylation
text:
Step 3: Normalization

# Noob + BMIQ normalization — recommended for EPIC
mSet <- preprocessNoob(rgSet)
mSet <- BMIQ(mSet)   # within-sample normalization

# Extract beta values (0–1, proportion methylated)
beta <- getBeta(mSet)

# Extract M-values (logit of beta, better for statistics)
mval <- getM(mSet)

# Beta values for visualization, M-values for statistical testing
cat("Beta matrix:", nrow(beta), "probes ×", ncol(beta), "samples\n")

title: Epigenomics I: DNA Methylation
text:
Step 4: Probe Filtering

library(maxprobes)   # cross-reactive probes list

# Remove probes that:
# 1. Failed QC in any sample
keep_probes <- rowSums(detP > 0.01) == 0

# 2. Are on sex chromosomes (if not studying sex differences)
annot <- getAnnotation(mSet)
keep_probes <- keep_probes & !(annot$chr %in% c("chrX", "chrY"))

# 3. Contain known SNPs at CpG site
keep_probes <- keep_probes & is.na(annot$Probe_maf)

# 4. Are known cross-reactive
xreact <- xreactive_probes(array_type = "EPIC")
keep_probes <- keep_probes & !(rownames(mSet) %in% xreact)

mSet_filtered <- mSet[keep_probes, ]
cat("Probes after filtering:", nrow(mSet_filtered), "\n")

title: Epigenomics I: DNA Methylation
text:
Step 5: Differential Methylation — DMPs

library(limma)

# Design matrix — adjust for age, sex, cell type composition
design <- model.matrix(
  ~ Group + age + sex + CD8T + CD4T + NK + Bcell + Mono + Gran,
  data = targets
)

# Fit linear model on M-values
fit <- lmFit(mval[keep_probes, ], design)
fit <- eBayes(fit)

# Extract DMPs
dmps <- topTable(fit,
                 coef    = "GroupCase",
                 number  = Inf,
                 sort.by = "p") |>
  as_tibble(rownames = "probe")

# Significant DMPs
sig_dmps <- dmps |>
  filter(adj.P.Val < 0.05, abs(logFC) > 0.1)

cat("Significant DMPs:", nrow(sig_dmps), "\n")

title: Epigenomics I: DNA Methylation
text:
Step 6: Differential Methylation — DMRs

library(DMRcate)

# DMR analysis — finds regions of co-methylated probes
myannotation <- cpg.annotate(
  object       = mval,
  datatype     = "array",
  what         = "M",
  analysis.type = "differential",
  design       = design,
  coef         = "GroupCase",
  arraytype    = "EPIC"
)

# Find DMRs
dmrcoutput <- dmrcate(myannotation,
                      lambda   = 1000,
                      C        = 2)

dmrs <- extractRanges(dmrcoutput, genome = "hg19")
dmrs

title: Epigenomics I: DNA Methylation
text:
Step 7: Visualization

library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)

# Volcano plot of DMPs
ggplot(dmps, aes(x = logFC, y = -log10(adj.P.Val))) +
  geom_point(aes(color = abs(logFC) > 0.1 & adj.P.Val < 0.05),
             alpha = 0.5, size = 0.8) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("gray70", "#D85A30")) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = -log10(0.05), linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(-0.1, 0.1), linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x     = "Δβ (M-value logFC)",
       y     = "-log10(adj. p-value)",
       title = "Differentially Methylated Positions",
       color = "Significant") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

text:
Cell Type Deconvolution — Critical Confounder

library(minfi)

# Whole blood methylation is a mixture of cell types
# Must estimate and correct for cell type composition

cell_counts <- estimateCellCounts2(

  pivot_longer(-sample, names_to = "cell_type", values_to = "proportion") |>
  ggplot(aes(sample, proportion, fill = cell_type)) +
  geom_col() +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Estimated blood cell type composition")

title: Epigenomics I: DNA Methylation
text:
Biological Age vs. Chronological Age

Horvath clock (2013) — multi-tissue, 353 CpGs → predicts chronological age
Hannum clock (2013) — blood-specific, 71 CpGs
PhenoAge (2018) — predicts mortality, not just age
GrimAge (2019) — predicts time-to-death and disease onset
DunedinPACE (2022) — pace of aging, not biological age point estimate


Epigenetic age acceleration = (biological age) − (chronological age)
Positive acceleration → aging faster → higher mortality, disease risk

title: Epigenomics I: DNA Methylation
text:
Computing Epigenetic Age

library(methylclock)

# Compute multiple epigenetic clocks at once
clocks <- DNAmAge(
  x        = beta,           # beta value matrix (probes × samples)
  clocks   = c("Horvath",
               "Hannum",
               "PhenoAge",
               "GrimAge"),
  cell.count = TRUE          # adjust for cell composition
)

# Age acceleration
clocks <- clocks |>
  mutate(
    AgeAccel_Horvath  = Horvath - age,
    AgeAccel_Hannum   = Hannum  - age,
    AgeAccel_PhenoAge = PhenoAge - age
  )

# Do cases age faster?
t.test(AgeAccel_GrimAge ~ Group, data = clocks)

title: Metagenomics I: 16S rRNA-seq
text:
You Are Not Alone

~38 trillion microbial cells in/on the human body (~1:1 with human cells)
~3.3 million microbial genes (vs. ~20,000 human protein-coding genes)
99% of the microbiome is in the gut
Collectively called the gut microbiome or gut flora


Clinically relevant in: IBD, IBS, colorectal cancer, T2D, obesity, cardiovascular disease,
mental health (gut–brain axis), autoimmune disease, drug metabolism,
immunotherapy response

title: Metagenomics I: 16S rRNA-seq
section: Why This Matters for Drug Response
text:
Why This Matters for Drug Response

Irinotecan (CPT-11) — gut bacteria reactivate the drug in the colon → diarrhea
Checkpoint inhibitors — Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, Akkermansia associated with response
Metformin — microbiome mediates glycemic effects
Antibiotics → dysbiosis → C. difficile → CDI








The gut–immunotherapy connection


Patients with high Akkermansia muciniphila abundance respond significantly better to anti-PD1 therapy.
This has been replicated in multiple cohorts across multiple tumor types.

title: Metagenomics I: 16S rRNA-seq
text:
Why 16S rRNA?
16S rRNA gene:
├── Conserved regions  → universal PCR primers
└── Variable regions   → species identification
    (V1-V2, V3-V4, V4 most common)

Workflow:
Stool/swab DNA → PCR amplify V3-V4 → Sequence → Assign taxonomy

Pros: Cheap (~$50/sample), easy, large reference databases
Cons: Amplification bias, ~genus level resolution, no functional info
→ For functional metagenomics: Whole Metagenome Shotgun (WMS) — next week (W7)

title: Metagenomics I: 16S rRNA-seq
text:
ASV vs. OTU — Modern Standard
OTU (Operational Taxonomic Unit) — old approach: - Cluster reads at 97% similarity → OTU table - Information loss, not reproducible
ASV (Amplicon Sequence Variant) — current standard (DADA2): - Exact sequence variants, corrected for sequencing errors - Reproducible across studies - Higher resolution (can distinguish strains)


Always use DADA2 / ASVs for new studies.
QIIME2 wraps DADA2 — both acceptable.

title: Metagenomics I: 16S rRNA-seq
text:
Analysis Workflow
Raw paired-end FASTQ (R1 + R2)
    │
    ├── 1. Quality inspection   → plotQualityProfile()
    ├── 2. Filtering & trimming → filterAndTrim()
    ├── 3. Error learning       → learnErrors()
    ├── 4. Denoising (DADA2)   → dada()
    ├── 5. Merging pairs        → mergePairs()
    ├── 6. Chimera removal      → removeBimeraDenovo()
    ├── 7. Taxonomy assignment  → assignTaxonomy() → SILVA
    └── 8. Phyloseq object      → diversity, composition analysis

title: Metagenomics I: 16S rRNA-seq
text:
Step 1: Quality Profiles

library(dada2)
library(here)

# List raw FASTQ files
fnFs <- sort(list.files(here("data", "raw", "fastq"),
                         pattern = "_R1_001.fastq.gz",
                         full.names = TRUE))
fnRs <- sort(list.files(here("data", "raw", "fastq"),
                         pattern = "_R2_001.fastq.gz",
                         full.names = TRUE))

sample_names <- sub("_R1_001.fastq.gz", "",
                    basename(fnFs))

# Visualize quality profiles
plotQualityProfile(fnFs[1:2])   # forward reads
plotQualityProfile(fnRs[1:2])   # reverse reads
# Quality usually drops at end of reads — decide truncation point

title: Metagenomics I: 16S rRNA-seq
text:
Step 2: Filter & Trim

# Output paths
filtFs <- file.path(here("data", "processed", "filtered"),
                    paste0(sample_names, "_F_filt.fastq.gz"))
filtRs <- file.path(here("data", "processed", "filtered"),
                    paste0(sample_names, "_R_filt.fastq.gz"))

# Filter — adjust truncLen based on quality profile
out <- filterAndTrim(
  fnFs, filtFs, fnRs, filtRs,
  truncLen    = c(240, 200),   # forward, reverse
  maxN        = 0,             # no Ns allowed
  maxEE       = c(2, 2),       # max expected errors
  truncQ      = 2,
  rm.phix     = TRUE,
  compress    = TRUE,
  multithread = TRUE
)

head(out)
# Check: >70% reads should pass filter

title: Metagenomics I: 16S rRNA-seq
text:
Step 3–4: Learn Errors & Denoise

# Learn error rates (takes ~10 min on 20 samples)
errF <- learnErrors(filtFs, multithread = TRUE)
errR <- learnErrors(filtRs, multithread = TRUE)

# Visualize error model — points should follow the line
plotErrors(errF, nominalQ = TRUE)

# DADA2 denoising — the core step
dadaFs <- dada(filtFs, err = errF, multithread = TRUE,
               pool = "pseudo")   # pool for rare ASVs
dadaRs <- dada(filtRs, err = errR, multithread = TRUE,
               pool = "pseudo")

dadaFs[[1]]
# dada-class: 128 sample sequences

title: Metagenomics I: 16S rRNA-seq
section: Step 5–7: Merge, Remove Chimeras, Assign Taxonomy
text:
Step 5–7: Merge, Remove Chimeras, Assign Taxonomy

# Merge paired reads
mergers <- mergePairs(dadaFs, filtFs,
                      dadaRs, filtRs,
                      verbose = TRUE)

# Make sequence table
seqtab <- makeSequenceTable(mergers)

# Inspect ASV length distribution — should center on ~253 bp (V3-V4)
table(nchar(getSequences(seqtab)))

# Remove chimeras
seqtab_nochim <- removeBimeraDenovo(seqtab,
                                    method     = "consensus",
                                    multithread = TRUE,
                                    verbose    = TRUE)

# Fraction of reads retained
sum(seqtab_nochim) / sum(seqtab)

title: Metagenomics I: 16S rRNA-seq
text:
Taxonomy Assignment

# SILVA database (download v138.1 from https://zenodo.org/record/4587955)
taxa <- assignTaxonomy(
  seqtab_nochim,
  here("data", "raw", "silva_nr99_v138.1_train_set.fa.gz"),
  multithread = TRUE
)

# Add species-level assignment
taxa <- addSpecies(
  taxa,
  here("data", "raw", "silva_species_assignment_v138.1.fa.gz")
)

# Preview
taxa_df <- as.data.frame(taxa)
head(taxa_df)
# Kingdom  Phylum          Class     Order      Family     Genus   Species
# Bacteria Bacteroidota    ...

title: Metagenomics I: 16S rRNA-seq
text:
Track Reads Through Pipeline

getN <- function(x) sum(getUniques(x))

track <- cbind(
  out,
  sapply(dadaFs, getN),
  sapply(dadaRs, getN),
  sapply(mergers, getN),
  rowSums(seqtab_nochim)
)

colnames(track) <- c("input", "filtered", "denoisedF",
                      "denoisedR", "merged", "nonchim")
rownames(track) <- sample_names

head(track)
# Should retain >70% from input to nonchim
# Large drops at merge → primer trimming needed
# Large drops at chimera → primer length issues

title: Metagenomics I: 16S rRNA-seq
text:
Building the phyloseq Object

library(phyloseq)
library(tidyverse)
library(here)

# Load sample metadata
metadata <- read_tsv(here("data", "raw", "sample_metadata.tsv")) |>
  column_to_rownames("sample_id")

# Build phyloseq object
ps <- phyloseq(
  otu_table(seqtab_nochim, taxa_are_rows = FALSE),
  sample_data(metadata),
  tax_table(taxa)
)

# Rename ASVs to short names
dna <- Biostrings::DNAStringSet(taxa_names(ps))
names(dna) <- paste0("ASV", seq(ntaxa(ps)))
taxa_names(ps) <- names(dna)

ps

title: Metagenomics I: 16S rRNA-seq
text:
Alpha Diversity — Within-Sample Diversity

# Rarefy to equal depth first
ps_rare <- rarefy_even_depth(ps,
                              sample.size = min(sample_sums(ps)),
                              rngseed     = 42)

# Alpha diversity metrics
alpha_div <- estimate_richness(ps_rare,
                                measures = c("Observed",
                                             "Shannon",
                                             "Simpson",
                                             "Chao1"))

alpha_div <- alpha_div |>
  rownames_to_column("sample_id") |>
  left_join(as(sample_data(ps), "data.frame") |>
            rownames_to_column("sample_id"))

# Compare between groups
ggplot(alpha_div, aes(x = Group, y = Shannon, fill = Group)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.1) +
  stat_compare_means() +
  labs(title = "Shannon diversity by group") +
  theme_minimal()

title: Metagenomics I: 16S rRNA-seq
text:
Beta Diversity — Between-Sample Diversity

library(vegan)

# Bray-Curtis dissimilarity — most common for microbiome
bray_dist <- distance(ps_rare, method = "bray")

# PCoA ordination
ord_pcoa <- ordinate(ps_rare, method = "PCoA",
                      distance = bray_dist)

# Plot
plot_ordination(ps_rare, ord_pcoa,
                color = "Group",
                shape = "Group") +
  geom_point(size = 3, alpha = 0.8) +
  stat_ellipse() +
  labs(title = "PCoA — Bray-Curtis dissimilarity") +
  theme_minimal()

# PERMANOVA — is the group difference significant?
adonis2(bray_dist ~ Group + age + sex,
        data = as(sample_data(ps_rare), "data.frame"),
        permutations = 999)

title: Metagenomics I: 16S rRNA-seq
text:
Differential Abundance — DESeq2 for Microbiome

library(DESeq2)

# Note: do NOT rarefy before DESeq2 — use raw counts
ps_deseq <- phyloseq_to_deseq2(ps, ~ Group)
ps_deseq <- DESeq(ps_deseq, test = "Wald",
                   fitType = "parametric")

res <- results(ps_deseq, cooksCutoff = FALSE)
res <- res[order(res$padj), ]

# Significant ASVs
sig_asvs <- res |>
  as_tibble(rownames = "ASV") |>
  filter(!is.na(padj), padj < 0.05) |>
  left_join(as.data.frame(tax_table(ps)) |>
            rownames_to_column("ASV"))

sig_asvs |> select(ASV, Genus, Species, log2FoldChange, padj)

# Relative abundance bar chart — collapse to genus level
ps_genus <- tax_glom(ps_rare, taxrank = "Genus")
ps_rel   <- transform_sample_counts(ps_genus,
                                     function(x) x / sum(x))

# Top 15 genera

                          decreasing = TRUE))[1:15]
ps_top <- prune_taxa(top_genera, ps_rel)

plot_bar(ps_top, fill = "Genus") +
  facet_wrap(~ Group, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(title = "Relative abundance — top 15 genera") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90))

title: Single-cell RNA-seq Fundamentals: Cell-type Specificity
text:
The Problem with Bulk RNA-seq
From last semester — bulk RNA-seq:
Tumor biopsy → homogenize → RNA → counts per gene

Gene X: 150 counts

But what does that mean?
Tumor cell A:    ████████  (high expression)
Tumor cell B:    ██        (medium)
Macrophage:      ████████  (high — confounding!)
Fibroblast:      ░░        (zero)
T cell:          ░░        (zero)

Bulk average: ████  ← misleading

title: Single-cell RNA-seq Fundamentals: Cell-type Specificity
text:
What scRNA-seq Resolves

Every cell gets its own expression profile
Identify cell types without prior knowledge
Find rare cell populations (<1% of tissue)
Discover cell states within a cell type
Map gene expression heterogeneity within tumors
Connect to GWAS — in which cell type is the risk gene expressed?



scRNA-seq is now standard in Nature/Cell/Science papers.
As a clinician-scientist, you need to be able to interpret and run these analyses.

title: Single-cell RNA-seq Fundamentals: Cell-type Specificity
text:
How 10x Chromium Works
Single-cell suspension
    ↓
Microfluidic droplet formation
(one cell + one bead + oil → GEM)
    ↓
Cell barcoding + UMI tagging
    ↓
cDNA synthesis + amplification
    ↓
Library sequencing
    ↓
Cell Ranger → count matrix
(cells × genes)

title: Single-cell RNA-seq Fundamentals: Cell-type Specificity
text:
The scRNA-seq Count Matrix
         Gene1  Gene2  Gene3  Gene4  ...
Cell_1      0      3      0     12
Cell_2      5      0      8      0
Cell_3      0      0      1      0
Cell_4      2      7      0      6
...

n_cells: 5,000–50,000
n_genes: ~20,000 (but 80–90% are zeros → sparse matrix)

The sparsity problem:
Each cell captures only ~5–15% of all transcripts → lots of zeros
This is a technical artifact (“dropout”) not true zero expression

title: Single-cell RNA-seq Fundamentals: Cell-type Specificity
text:
Overview
Cell Ranger output (barcodes, features, matrix)
    │
    ├── 1. Load & create Seurat object
    ├── 2. QC → filter low-quality cells
    ├── 3. Normalization → SCTransform
    ├── 4. Feature selection → highly variable genes
    ├── 5. Scaling & PCA
    ├── 6. Clustering → FindNeighbors + FindClusters
    ├── 7. UMAP visualization
    ├── 8. Marker gene identification
    └── 9. Cell type annotation → SingleR / manual

title: Single-cell RNA-seq Fundamentals: Cell-type Specificity
text:
Step 1: Load Data

library(Seurat)
library(tidyverse)
library(here)

# Load 10x Cell Ranger output
counts <- Read10X(data.dir = here("data", "raw",
                                   "cellranger_output",
                                   "filtered_feature_bc_matrix"))

# Create Seurat object
seurat <- CreateSeuratObject(
  counts    = counts,
  project   = "PBMC",
  min.cells = 3,      # gene must be in ≥3 cells
  min.features = 200  # cell must have ≥200 genes
)

seurat
# 23,000 features × 8,000 samples (cells)

title: Single-cell RNA-seq Fundamentals: Cell-type Specificity
text:
Step 2: QC — Three Key Metrics

  seurat,
  PCs          = 1:30,

Pseudobulk — The Right Way

library(DESeq2)

# Wrong: treat each cell as independent observation → inflated p-values
# Right: aggregate cells per sample → pseudobulk → DESeq2

# Aggregate counts per cell type per sample
pseudobulk <- AggregateExpression(
  seurat,
  group.by     = c("cell_type", "sample_id"),
  assays       = "RNA",
  return.seurat = FALSE
)

# For each cell type, run DESeq2
run_pseudobulk_de <- function(cell_type_name, seurat_obj) {
  cells <- subset(seurat_obj, cell_type == cell_type_name)

  bulk  <- AggregateExpression(cells,
                                group.by   = "sample_id",
                                assays     = "RNA")$RNA

  meta  <- cells@meta.data |>
    distinct(sample_id, .keep_all = TRUE) |>
    column_to_rownames("sample_id")

  dds   <- DESeqDataSetFromMatrix(bulk, meta, ~ condition)
  dds   <- DESeq(dds)
  results(dds)
}

de_cd8 <- run_pseudobulk_de("CD8 T cell", seurat)

title: Multi-omics Integration & GWAS Gene Prioritization
text:
The MOFA2 Idea
Omics layer 1: RNA-seq    (n_samples × n_genes)
Omics layer 2: Methylation (n_samples × n_CpGs)
Omics layer 3: Metabolomics (n_samples × n_metabolites)
         ↓
MOFA2: find latent factors that explain variance ACROSS layers

Factor 1 → driven by cell cycle genes + methylation changes
Factor 2 → driven by immune activity in RNA + microbiome
Factor 3 → driven by metabolic genes + metabolites

Each factor = a biological axis of variation shared across omics layers

title: Multi-omics Integration & GWAS Gene Prioritization
text:
DIABLO — Multi-block Discriminant Analysis
Goal: find a combination of features across omics layers
      that best discriminates between groups (e.g., responder vs. non-responder)

Input:
  X = list of omics matrices (RNA, methylation, proteomics)
  Y = outcome variable (factor: responder / non-responder)

Output:
  - Selected features per layer
  - Correlation structure between layers
  - Classification model

title: Multi-omics Integration & GWAS Gene Prioritization
text:
Running DIABLO

library(mixOmics)

# Input data
X <- list(
  RNA    = t(rna_filtered),      # samples × features
  Methyl = t(meth_filtered),
  Micro  = t(micro_filtered)
)
Y <- factor(sample_metadata$response)   # "Responder" / "Non-responder"

# Design matrix — how correlated should layers be?
# 1 = maximize inter-layer correlation
# 0 = maximize discrimination only
design <- matrix(0.1,
                  ncol = length(X),
                  nrow = length(X),
                  dimnames = list(names(X), names(X)))
diag(design) <- 0

# Initial DIABLO run
diablo <- block.splsda(X, Y,
                        ncomp  = 5,
                        design = design)

title: Multi-omics Integration & GWAS Gene Prioritization
text:
Tuning & Final Model

# Tune number of features to select per layer
set.seed(42)
perf_diablo <- perf(diablo,
                     validation    = "Mfold",
                     folds         = 5,
                     nrepeat       = 10,
                     dist          = "centroids.dist")

# Optimal number of components
plot(perf_diablo)
ncomp_opt <- perf_diablo$choice.ncomp$WeightedVote["Overall.BER",
                                                     "centroids.dist"]

# Tune number of features
test_keepX <- list(RNA    = c(5, 10, 15, 20),
                   Methyl = c(5, 10, 15),
                   Micro  = c(3, 5, 10))

tune_diablo <- tune.block.splsda(X, Y,
                                  ncomp      = ncomp_opt,
                                  test.keepX = test_keepX,
                                  design     = design,
                                  validation = "Mfold",
                                  folds      = 5,
                                  nrepeat    = 10)

# Final model
final_diablo <- block.splsda(X, Y,
                              ncomp    = ncomp_opt,
                              keepX    = tune_diablo$choice.keepX,
                              design   = design)

text:
The Problem: GWAS Hit → Causal Gene
A GWAS locus typically contains: - 1 lead SNP - Dozens of correlated SNPs in LD - Multiple nearby genes
Which gene is the actual effector?
Evidence layers for gene prioritization:
├── Positional     → nearest gene
├── eQTL           → gene whose expression is controlled by the SNP
├── Chromatin      → SNP overlaps enhancer contacting gene X (Hi-C)
├── Epigenomic     → SNP in cell-type-specific open chromatin
├── scRNA-seq      → gene expressed in disease-relevant cell type
└── Multi-omics    → gene appears across multiple evidence layers

text:
Why Visualization Matters

A great analysis with bad figures doesn’t get published
A mediocre analysis with compelling figures gets attention
Reviewers form first impressions from Figure 1 before reading methods
For your capstone: your hypothesis lives or dies by how clearly you present it



The figure is the argument. The methods section just explains how you got there.

title: Data Interpretation & Visualization
text:
The Five Principles

One message per panel — don’t overload a single plot
Direct labeling over legends — reduce eye travel
Color encodes meaning — don’t use color just to be colorful
Whitespace is not wasted — clutter kills clarity
Think about the reader’s path — A → B → C

title: Data Interpretation & Visualization
text:
The Grammar of Graphics Mindset

library(ggplot2)
library(tidyverse)
library(here)

# Everything in ggplot2 is a layer
ggplot(data, aes(x, y)) +          # data + aesthetics
  geom_point() +                    # geometry
  stat_smooth(method = "lm") +      # statistical transformation
  scale_color_manual(...) +         # scale
  facet_wrap(~ group) +             # facet
  labs(title = "...", x = "...") +  # labels
  theme_minimal()                    # theme








Build plots incrementally


Start with ggplot(data, aes()) + geom_point().
Add one layer at a time. Print after each addition.
Never write a 20-line ggplot in one go without checking.

title: Data Interpretation & Visualization
text:
Volcano Plot — Publication Ready

library(ggplot2)
library(ggrepel)

# Assume: de_results from DESeq2
de_results <- de_results |>
  mutate(
    status = case_when(
      padj < 0.05 & log2FoldChange >  1 ~ "Up",
      padj < 0.05 & log2FoldChange < -1 ~ "Down",
      TRUE                               ~ "NS"
    ),
    label = ifelse(padj < 1e-10 | abs(log2FoldChange) > 3,
                   gene, NA)
  )

ggplot(de_results, aes(x = log2FoldChange,
                        y = -log10(padj),
                        color = status)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6, size = 0.8) +
  geom_text_repel(aes(label = label),
                   size     = 3,
                   max.overlaps = 20,
                   box.padding  = 0.3) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(Up   = "#D85A30",
                                 Down = "#185FA5",
                                 NS   = "gray70")) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = -log10(0.05),
             linetype = "dashed", color = "gray40") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(-1, 1),
             linetype = "dashed", color = "gray40") +
  labs(x     = "log₂ fold change",
       y     = "-log₁₀(adjusted p-value)",
       color = "",
       title = "Differential expression — Case vs. Control") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "top",
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank())

title: Data Interpretation & Visualization
text:
Heatmap — ComplexHeatmap

library(ComplexHeatmap)
library(circlize)

# Color scale — always center on 0 for scaled data
col_fun <- colorRamp2(c(-2, 0, 2),
                       c("#185FA5", "white", "#D85A30"))

# Column annotation
ha <- HeatmapAnnotation(
  Group    = sample_metadata$group,
  Age      = sample_metadata$age,
  col      = list(
    Group = c(Control = "#1D9E75", Case = "#D85A30"),
    Age   = colorRamp2(c(20, 80), c("white", "#534AB7"))
  ),
  annotation_name_side = "left"
)

# Main heatmap
ht <- Heatmap(
  scaled_matrix,
  name                    = "z-score",
  col                     = col_fun,
  top_annotation          = ha,
  show_column_names       = FALSE,
  clustering_distance_rows = "pearson",
  clustering_method_rows  = "ward.D2",
  row_names_gp            = gpar(fontsize = 8),
  border                  = TRUE,
  row_title               = "Top DE genes"
)

draw(ht, heatmap_legend_side = "right")

title: Data Interpretation & Visualization
text:
Combining Plots — patchwork

library(patchwork)

# Build individual panels
p1 <- ggplot(data, aes(group, expression, fill = group)) +
  geom_boxplot() + labs(tag = "A")

p2 <- ggplot(umap_df, aes(UMAP_1, UMAP_2, color = cell_type)) +
  geom_point(size = 0.5) + labs(tag = "B")

p3 <- ggplot(de_results, aes(log2FoldChange, -log10(padj))) +
  geom_point() + labs(tag = "C")

p4 <- ggplot(pathway_df, aes(NES, pathway)) +
  geom_col() + labs(tag = "D")

# Combine into figure layout
(p1 | p2) /
(p3 | p4) +
  plot_layout(guides = "collect") &
  theme(legend.position = "right")

# Save as high-resolution PDF
ggsave(here("results", "figures", "figure1.pdf"),
       width = 10, height = 8,
       device = cairo_pdf)

text:
Color — The Most Misused Element

library(RColorBrewer)
library(ggsci)     # Nature, Science, NEJM color palettes

# For categorical data — colorblind-friendly
scale_color_manual(values = c(
  "#0072B2",   # blue
  "#D55E00",   # orange
  "#009E73",   # green
  "#CC79A7",   # pink
  "#E69F00",   # yellow
  "#56B4E9",   # light blue
  "#F0E442"    # yellow (use sparingly)
))

# For sequential data
scale_fill_distiller(palette = "Blues", direction = 1)

# For diverging data (fold change, correlation)
scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#185FA5", mid = "white",
                      high = "#D85A30", midpoint = 0)

# Nature journal palette
scale_color_npg()    # ggsci::scale_color_npg()

# NEJM palette
scale_color_nejm()

Dot Plot for Pathway Results

# Better than bar charts for enrichment results
pathway_df |>
  slice_max(abs(NES), n = 20) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = NES,
             y = reorder(pathway, NES),
             size  = setSize,
             color = padj)) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_color_gradient(low  = "#D85A30",
                       high = "gray80",
                       name = "adj. p-value",
                       trans = "log10") +
  scale_size_continuous(range = c(2, 8),
                        name  = "Gene set size") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x     = "Normalized enrichment score (NES)",
       y     = "",
       title = "GSEA — top pathways") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_line(color = "gray90"))

title: Data Interpretation & Visualization
text:
Panel Layout Principles

# Use consistent sizing
# Journal column widths:
# Single column: 3.5 inches
# 1.5 column:    5 inches
# Double column: 7 inches

# Always set figure size explicitly in ggsave
ggsave(
  filename = here("results", "figures", "fig2.pdf"),
  plot     = my_figure,
  width    = 7,      # double column
  height   = 5,
  units    = "in",
  device   = cairo_pdf   # for proper font embedding
)

# For raster formats (e.g., presentations):
ggsave(
  filename = here("results", "figures", "fig2.png"),
  plot     = my_figure,
  width    = 7,
  height   = 5,
  dpi      = 300    # minimum for publication
)

title: Data Interpretation & Visualization
text:
The Axis Trap

# BAD: truncated y-axis exaggerates differences
ggplot(data, aes(group, value)) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(95, 102))   # NEVER do this

# GOOD: start from 0 for bar charts
ggplot(data, aes(group, value)) +
  geom_col() +
  expand_limits(y = 0)

# Exception: show variation when absolute value is less important
# (e.g., gene expression changes) → boxplot / violinplot, not bar
ggplot(data, aes(group, expression)) +
  geom_violin(aes(fill = group)) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.1, fill = "white") +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.05, alpha = 0.3, size = 0.5)

title: Data Interpretation & Visualization
text:
Statistical Annotation

library(ggpubr)
library(rstatix)

# Compute statistics
stat_test <- data |>
  t_test(expression ~ group) |>
  add_significance() |>
  add_xy_position(x = "group")

# Add to plot
ggplot(data, aes(group, expression, fill = group)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.1, alpha = 0.5, size = 1) +
  stat_pvalue_manual(stat_test,
                     label     = "p.adj.signif",
                     tip.length = 0.01) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#1D9E75", "#D85A30")) +
  labs(y = "Expression (normalized)") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

title: Data Interpretation & Visualization
text:
What Must Be Reported

Sample sizes — always, for every group
Statistical tests — name the test, not just “p < 0.05”
Multiple testing correction — BH, Bonferroni — which and why
Effect sizes — OR, HR, log2FC — not just p-values
Software versions — R version + package versions (sessionInfo())
Data availability — GEO accession numbers, GitHub code repository
Reproducibility — seeds set, renv snapshot included

title: Data Interpretation & Visualization
text:
Good Capstone Questions (Examples)

“Do patients with high PRS for T2D show distinct gut microbiome composition in the HMP2 cohort?”
“Which cell types express the top AD GWAS genes, and do they show altered states in disease?”
“Can CMAP identify drugs that reverse the transcriptomic signature of senescent cardiomyocytes?”
“Are GWAS hits for IBD enriched in open chromatin of intestinal epithelial cells vs. immune cells?”








Keep it focused


One question, one dataset, two methods.
A clean answer to a focused question is better than a messy tour of everything.
